title: Partial Token Streaming Protocol (draft)
body:
Purpose
This doc captures a proposed protocol and implementation guidance for streaming generation internals: token chunking, flush policies, cancellation semantics, partial-token frames, and interaction with KV cache and scheduling. Goal is to reduce client-observed latency while preserving correctness (no token duplication or re-order) and ensuring operational safety for batching and kernel execution.

Background & constraints
- Serving runtime is GPU-bound and uses batching and kernel-level optimizations. A single request's tokens may be produced across many micro-batches.
- Clients expect low time-to-first-byte and progressive token emission for UX.
- We must avoid KV-cache divergence between instances/variants; decisions to persist KV state must be deterministic relative to emitted tokens.
- Cancellations can be initiated by client, but we still may prefer to emit a final flush to surface the last partial token(s).

Design principles
1) Deterministic token boundaries: only tokens that are produced and confirmed as "final" advance the committed KV cursor. Partial-token frames are allowed for UX but do not change KV commit state.
2) Low-latency flush: flush frequently for the first N tokens, then adaptively coalesce for throughput.
3) Scheduler-friendly: per-request streaming emissions must be compatible with cross-request batching. Kernel preemption should not cause re-emission of finalized tokens.
4) Minimal wire types: keep streaming frame types small and stable for clients.

Frame model (frame_type):
- token_partial: payload = UTF-8 bytes of partial token surface (may be byte-level or grapheme-level depending on tokenizer). Indicates token generation is in-progress.
- token_final: payload = finalized token string (this token is now committed; KV cursor advances).
- flush_hint: metadata-only frame from server indicating that buffered partials should be flushed soon (client can show spinner).
- eos: end-of-stream; finalizes request.
- cancelled: server acknowledges client cancellation.
- meta: delivery of non-token info (probabilities, alignments, reason codes).

Key invariants
- Only token_final affects KV cache commit state. Partial frames never update persistent KV state.
- token_final frames must be monotonic for a request; ordering preserved.
- If a token_final is sent, it must not be re-sent later for the same request id (idempotency guaranteed).

Chunking algorithm (producer side)
- Base unit: tokenizer token IDs (model tokenizer). However, to support UX, we also emit partial surface segments which correspond to sub-token byte/grapheme units. Implementation: keep token assembly buffer per-request. When model emits logits progressively for a token, convert emitted bytes to UTF-8 safe incremental surface and send token_partial.
- Thresholds: 
  - first-token aggressive flush: for tokens 0..2, flush partials every 5-10ms or after 1-2 bytes to reduce time-to-first-byte.
  - steady-state: emit partial only if > 4 bytes or > 40ms since last partial for that request.
  - size cap: never emit partial frames bigger than 256 bytes; if partial exceeds, send token_final if token complete or coalesce into multiple partial frames with sequence numbers.
- Backoff rules: if batching delay is expected (scheduler sets delay_hint), the streaming layer prefers to wait up to delay_hint before emitting partials to avoid high overhead of many tiny GPU wakeups.

Flush policy
- Two-layer flush: local-request flush and global-batching flush.
  - Local-request flush: when a token becomes final or partial-policy triggers, push to client socket with low latency.
  - Global-batching flush: scheduler may coalesce multiple requests and hold transmission for payload aggregation up to a configurable SLO (e.g., 15ms) to improve token throughput.
- Flush priority: token_final > token_partial > flush_hint. token_final always preempts batching windows (i.e., must be sent immediately).
- Explicit flush semantics on preemption: if kernel preemption would discard in-flight partials, runtime must convert latest partial into a token_final only if model state indicates token sampling has converged to top-k stable threshold (heuristic: sampling entropy below X). Otherwise, emit a partial indicating possible truncation and mark request resumed_flag = true.

Cancellation semantics
- Client cancels by sending a cancel/control frame with request_id. Server must acknowledge with cancelled frame.
- Best-effort finalization: upon cancellation receipt server will attempt to produce a best-effort token_final if: (a) token is near-final (entropy < threshold) or (b) partial buffering > time_budget_for_cancel (e.g., 20ms). This gives clients an MVS UX while letting server reclaim worker resources.
- KV cache on cancel: do NOT commit KV cursor for cancelled requests unless token_final was emitted and acknowledged by the client. If cancellation occurs after token_final, token_final semantics persist.

Partial token handling and client expectations
- Partial frames are advisory: rendering clients should combine sequential partial frames into a visible token surface but should not assume token is final until token_final arrives.
- If network reordering or reconnect happens, client can request last-acked-token-index; server will re-send token_final frames from that index onward. Partial frames are not re-sent.
- Sequence numbering: optional sequence_no field can be attached to partial/final frames for debugging and re-sync. Sequence numbers must be monotonically increasing for a request.

KV cache interaction and commit rules
- Commit point = index of last token_final acknowledged by the client (or by internal durable ack if using private deployment with control plane).
- The runtime must not evict KV entries required to re-generate any token_final that might be re-sent after reconnect. Keep window size >= max-rewind-tokens (default 32) for safety.
- When batching across model variants (quantized vs full), only route requests to fallback variant if the commit point is at a token boundary — we must ensure identical prefixes for determinism.

Scheduler & kernel implications
- Batching co-existence: scheduling should allow a low-latency lane (small batch targets) for streaming-first tokens. This lane will accept smaller batch sizes for earlier tokens and drain more frequently.
- Kernel preemption handling: model kernels must export a minimal snapshot API to allow safe stopping and resuming of partial token generation without duplicating final tokens. Runtime should prefer to pause generation between tokens; if interrupted mid-token, emit a token_partial and resume later.
- Quantization path divergence: some quantized kernels produce tokens faster but with drift in sampling probabilities. We must tie finalization to the same pseudo-random stream seed and sampling decisions to avoid divergence when falling back.

Wire format examples (JSON frames for clarity)
1) partial emission:
{
  "frame": "token_partial",
  "request_id": "r-23",
  "seq": "12",
  "text": "hel"
}
2) token finalized:
{
  "frame": "token_final",
  "request_id": "r-23",
  "seq": "13",
  "text": "hello",
  "token_id": "456"
}
3) cancel ack:
{
  "frame": "cancelled",
  "request_id": "r-23",
  "reason": "client_cancel"
}

Testing and metrics
- Unit tests: partial->final sequences; reconnects with last-acked-token-index; cancellation-before-final; kernel preemption integration tests.
- Integration tests: cross-batch ordering, KV window under heavy eviction pressure, fallback variant deterministic replays.
- Metrics to record per-request: time_to_first_partial, time_to_first_final, partial_frame_count, cancellations, resumed_after_preemption boolean, kv_commit_index, bytes_emitted. Create dashboards for 95th latency and partial-frame churn.

Migration and rollout plan
- Phase 0: feature gated in internal cluster with simulation harness; run head-to-head compare with current streaming behavior.
- Phase 1: enable for selected hosted-api customers and internal e2e tests; monitor regressions.
- Phase 2: default for all streaming responses with aggressive telemetry and automatic rollback on violation of latency/duplication SLOs.

Open questions
- How best to represent partial bytes for multi-byte UTF-8 tokenization in presence of byte-level sampling? (Option: always emit grapheme-sanitized partials).
- Exact entropy threshold for safe token_final conversion during preemption/cancel. Suggest experiments: sample across datasets and measure quality delta.
- Backpressure signalling: should clients be able to request flush frequency preferences? (privacy concerns + API complexity).

Appendix: quick checklist for implementer
- [ ] implement token buffer with partial->final demarcation per-request.
- [ ] expose sequence_no for debugging builds.
- [ ] add KV window reservation logic and eviction guard for streaming requests.
- [ ] scheduler: add low-latency lane and delay_hint propagation.
- [ ] tests and metrics as listed above.

Summary
This draft aims to standardize how the serving runtime emits partial and final tokens, how cancellation and preemption are handled, and how those behaviors interact with KV caching and the scheduler. It prioritizes deterministic KV commits, low latency UX for clients, and scheduler-level efficiency. Feedback requested: edge cases around multi-byte token partials, the cancel finalization heuristic, and interaction with cross-variant fallbacks.
